blocks.text: Infective endocarditis is a potentially fatal infection of the endocardial surface, most often involving heart valves, but it can also affect prosthetic valves, intracardiac devices or other endocardial structures. Treatment requires urgent hospital-based antimicrobial therapy, organism-directed prescribing, assessment for complications and early consideration of cardiac surgery.

The 2023 European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guideline and the American Heart Association's 2026 scientific statement are important contemporary references. Regimens must be adapted to culture results, susceptibility testing, renal function, allergy history, local antimicrobial resistance and specialist advice.

Safety warning: Suspected IE should not be managed with a routine short outpatient antibiotic course. Obtain appropriate blood cultures before antibiotics whenever this can be done without dangerous delay, admit or urgently refer the patient, and involve cardiology, infectious diseases/microbiology and cardiac surgery as indicated.

items.text: Eradicate the infecting organism with an appropriate bactericidal antimicrobial regimen.
Prevent progressive valve destruction, heart failure, abscesses and conduction abnormalities.
Reduce systemic embolisation and metastatic infection.
Identify patients who need urgent surgery or removal of infected prosthetic material or devices.
Prevent relapse through correct dose, route, duration, monitoring and follow-up.

Obtain three sets of peripheral blood cultures, ideally from separate venepunctures, before the first antibiotic dose when the patient is stable enough to permit this. Do not delay urgent antibiotics in sepsis or haemodynamic instability.
Use empiric therapy according to native versus prosthetic valve, community versus healthcare acquisition, previous antibiotics and local resistance.
Review preliminary microbiology results promptly and narrow therapy to the organism and susceptibility pattern as soon as possible.

Most patients initially need IV antibiotics and inpatient care. Selected stable patients may transition to outpatient parenteral or carefully selected oral therapy only after complications are controlled and specialist criteria are met.
Treatment duration is usually measured in weeks, not days. The exact course depends on the organism, valve type, complications and regimen.
Seek urgent cardiac surgical review for heart failure due to valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection or high risk of embolisation.

blocks.text: Empiric therapy should be started after cultures when feasible. There is no single regimen appropriate for every patient or hospital. The following are frameworks for clinician-led selection, not automatic prescriptions.

Coverage generally needs to include susceptible staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci. Depending on the clinical setting and local guidance, a specialist may select a beta-lactam-based combination such as:

items.text: Ampicillin plus ceftriaxone; or
An antistaphylococcal penicillin such as flucloxacillin, with additional agents selected according to the suspected pathogens and local protocol.

blocks.text: The choice depends on local MRSA prevalence, prior antibiotics, allergy history, renal function and microbiology advice. Do not add gentamicin routinely to every native-valve regimen: nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity are important risks, and its role depends on the specific organism and guideline.

blocks.title: These infections require urgent specialist input and broader consideration of:

items.text: Methicillin-resistant staphylococci, including coagulase-negative staphylococci.
Enterococci.
Healthcare-associated Gram-negative organisms where epidemiologically relevant.

blocks.text: The empiric regimen should be based on the timing of prosthetic valve surgery, prior healthcare exposure, previous antibiotics, local resistance patterns and suspected infection source. Regimens often use IV vancomycin or another appropriate anti-resistant Gram-positive agent together with additional coverage selected by the endocarditis team.

Do not automatically add rifampicin or gentamicin to every suspected prosthetic-valve infection. Their indications, timing, interactions and toxicity require organism-specific and specialist-directed decisions.

blocks.title: When IE is accompanied by septic shock or rapidly progressive organ dysfunction:

items.text: Obtain blood cultures immediately if this does not delay treatment.
Start appropriate IV antibiotics promptly according to the hospital sepsis protocol and suspected IE pathogens.
Provide haemodynamic support and critical care as indicated.
Seek urgent cardiology, microbiology/infectious diseases and cardiac surgery input.

blocks.text: The empiric regimen must cover the likely pathogens and be reviewed promptly as microbiology results become available.
Once the causative organism and susceptibility results are known, switch to the narrowest effective regimen consistent with the infection site, valve type and clinical course.
Common options for susceptible isolates

items.text: Benzylpenicillin (penicillin G): commonly 12–18 million units per 24 hours IV, divided every 4–6 hours or administered by continuous infusion according to the local protocol.
Ceftriaxone: commonly 2 g IV every 24 hours.

blocks.text: Duration: Often 4 weeks for native-valve disease with an appropriate regimen; prosthetic-valve infection usually requires a longer course. Selected uncomplicated cases may qualify for a shorter regimen under strict guideline criteria.
Confirm susceptibility, valve type, renal function and whether the chosen regimen is appropriate for the isolate.
Common options

items.text: Flucloxacillin: commonly 2 g IV every 4 hours in adults with normal renal function; or
Cefazolin: commonly 2 g IV every 8 hours, where appropriate.

blocks.text: Duration: Commonly 4–6 weeks, depending on valve type, complications and the treatment protocol.

For serious MSSA infection, an appropriate antistaphylococcal beta-lactam is generally preferred over vancomycin when the patient can safely receive it. Dose adjustment may be needed for renal impairment.
Common options

items.text: IV vancomycin with exposure-guided monitoring; or
High-dose IV daptomycin, commonly 10 mg/kg every 24 hours in selected adult regimens, with renal adjustment and specialist oversight.

blocks.text: Duration: Commonly 6 weeks, individualised to the valve type, complications and clinical response.
Vancomycin requires renal and drug-exposure monitoring. Daptomycin requires creatine kinase monitoring and assessment for myopathy; it is not suitable for treating pneumonia.
Common option for susceptible isolates

items.text: Ampicillin: commonly 2 g IV every 4 hours, plus
Ceftriaxone: commonly 2 g IV every 12 hours.

blocks.text: Duration: Often 6 weeks, particularly in prosthetic-valve infection or complicated disease.

This combination is frequently selected for susceptible E. faecalis IE because it provides synergistic activity while avoiding some of the renal toxicity associated with prolonged aminoglycoside-containing regimens. Confirm susceptibility and specialist recommendations.

These are standard adult examples, not universal regimens. The dose and duration must be adjusted for the organism, susceptibility profile, native versus prosthetic valve, renal function, complications and applicable guideline.
These examples illustrate prescription structure. Use them only after the organism, susceptibility, indication and patient-specific factors have been established.
Example regimen
Rx: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours.
Route: Intravenous infusion, prepared and administered according to the product instructions and institutional IV-antibiotic policy.
Duration: Commonly 4 weeks for an eligible native-valve case; determine the actual duration with the endocarditis team.
Quantity: For a planned 28-day course, 28 doses of 2 g are required. Hospital pharmacy must calculate the actual supply based on the preparation, stability and administration arrangements.
Monitoring: Allergy, clinical response, renal/hepatic function where indicated, blood counts for prolonged treatment, and microbiological response.
Example regimen
Rx: Flucloxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours in an adult with normal renal function, where the isolate is susceptible and the regimen is appropriate.
Duration: Commonly 4–6 weeks; establish the exact course with specialist input.
Administration: Use the hospital's approved IV preparation and infusion protocol. Do not assume all concentrations, diluents or infusion durations are interchangeable.
Monitoring: Allergy, renal function, full blood count, liver tests as indicated and clinical response.
Example regimen
Rx 1: Ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours.
Rx 2: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours.
Duration: Often 6 weeks, subject to the susceptibility profile, valve type and specialist plan.
Monitoring: Renal function, blood counts, liver tests as indicated, allergy and clinical/microbiological response. Check compatibility and line-management instructions before co-administration.

Prescription safety: For a prolonged IV regimen, the prescription and discharge plan should state the organism, dose, route, interval, intended treatment end date, renal adjustment plan, line-care arrangements, laboratory monitoring and who is responsible for reviewing results.
Endocarditis treatment often involves frequent, prolonged IV administration. Pharmacy and nursing teams should verify preparation details for each product.

blocks.text: Never assume that two IV antibiotics can be mixed in the same syringe, bag or line. Verify compatibility, dilution, stability and flushing instructions through the hospital pharmacy or approved IV compatibility resource.

blocks.text: For serious MRSA infection, use an institutionally approved exposure-guided approach, preferably AUC-based monitoring when available. The target used for serious MRSA infections should follow the applicable specialist protocol. A trough concentration alone may not accurately represent exposure and can increase toxicity if used as the sole target.

Do not use a fixed gentamicin regimen without checking the indication, body weight, renal function and monitoring requirements. If indicated, specify the dose, interval, level-sampling plan and stop/review date. Prolonged treatment can cause irreversible hearing or balance damage as well as renal injury.

Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer and can substantially reduce the effect of medicines including warfarin and some antiretrovirals. It should not be added casually to empiric IE therapy. Use only when indicated by the organism, infected material and specialist protocol.
Negative blood cultures do not exclude IE. Important reasons include prior antibiotics, fastidious organisms, inadequate sampling and non-infectious conditions that mimic infection.

items.text: Review the number and timing of cultures and previous antibiotic exposure.
Consult microbiology or infectious diseases specialists.
Consider targeted serology and molecular testing for relevant fastidious pathogens, guided by epidemiology and exposure.
Reassess imaging and diagnostic evidence.
Select empiric treatment based on the suspected cause, prior antibiotics, valve type and local epidemiology.

blocks.text: Do not keep broad-spectrum antibiotics unchanged indefinitely without revisiting the diagnosis and microbiological evidence.

subsections.subsection_title: 10. Treatment duration and the start date

blocks.text: Treatment is generally prolonged because organisms within vegetations can be difficult to eradicate.

items.text: Native-valve IE commonly requires around 2–6 weeks, depending on the pathogen and regimen.
Prosthetic-valve IE commonly requires at least 6 weeks.
Some organisms, complications or surgical findings require a longer or specifically tailored course.
Short-course treatment is appropriate only for selected patients meeting strict criteria.

blocks.text: The date used to calculate the treatment course depends on the clinical scenario, culture clearance, organism, regimen and whether surgery occurs. It should be explicitly documented by the endocarditis team rather than automatically calculated from the admission date.
Outpatient IV or oral step-down treatment is reserved for carefully selected clinically stable patients after relevant complications have been excluded or controlled.

subsections.subsection_title: 11. When antibiotics alone are not enough: surgery and source control

blocks.text: Urgent cardiac surgical assessment is essential when any of the following are present:

items.text: Acute heart failure due to severe valve dysfunction.
Persistent infection, abscess, fistula or other uncontrolled local infection despite appropriate antibiotics.
Recurrent embolisation or vegetations associated with a high embolic risk.
Prosthetic-valve complications or infection involving an intracardiac device.
Severe valve obstruction or regurgitation causing haemodynamic compromise.

blocks.text: Emergency surgery may be required for refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock caused by valve dysfunction. Surgery is not automatically delayed until the antibiotic course is completed when a life-threatening indication is present.

For cardiac implantable electronic device infection, complete device removal is often necessary when infection is established; antibiotic therapy alone may fail if infected hardware remains. Decisions should be made by the relevant specialist team.
IE is not itself an indication to start anticoagulation.

items.text: Do not initiate anticoagulation solely to prevent septic emboli from vegetations.
A patient already taking anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation, a mechanical valve or venous thromboembolism requires an individualised plan.
Intracranial haemorrhage, ischaemic stroke, infective aneurysm, planned surgery and prosthetic valve status can materially alter the decision.
Do not automatically stop or continue anticoagulation in every case; involve cardiology, neurology and cardiac surgery as appropriate.

blocks.text: Worsening heart failure, persistent positive cultures, new conduction abnormalities, new embolic events or clinical deterioration should trigger urgent reassessment for uncontrolled infection or a surgical complication.

blocks.title: Before discharge or transition to outpatient treatment, ensure:

items.text: The pathogen and susceptibility profile are documented, or a specialist plan exists for culture-negative disease.
The full antimicrobial regimen and end date are written clearly.
The patient is clinically stable and relevant complications have been addressed.
Any required IV line, administration service and line-care arrangements are established.
Laboratory monitoring and responsibility for reviewing results are specified.
Cardiology/infectious diseases follow-up is arranged.
The patient knows to seek urgent care for breathlessness, recurrent fever, neurological symptoms, severe bleeding or other deterioration.
Oral health and future endocarditis prevention are addressed where relevant.

blocks.text: Antibiotic prophylaxis is recommended only for selected patients at highest risk of adverse outcomes undergoing specific procedures, especially certain dental procedures involving gingival manipulation, the periapical region of teeth or oral mucosal perforation. It is not recommended routinely for every patient with a murmur or every dental procedure.

The eligibility criteria and regimen should follow current national guidance. Patients with previous IE, certain prosthetic valves or prosthetic valve-repair material, and selected congenital heart conditions are among groups that may qualify. Good oral hygiene and regular dental care are important for prevention.

items.text: Take blood cultures before antibiotics when feasible, but do not delay urgent treatment in an unstable patient.
Narrow empiric therapy as soon as reliable microbiology results become available.
Use prolonged, susceptibility-directed treatment; do not treat IE as uncomplicated bacteraemia.
Avoid routine gentamicin for every native-valve case because toxicity can outweigh benefit.
Rifampicin has a specific role in selected infections involving prosthetic material; it is not a universal addition.
MSSA IE is generally treated with an appropriate antistaphylococcal beta-lactam when tolerated.
High-dose daptomycin requires CK and renal monitoring.
Persistent infection, heart failure or embolic complications require assessment for surgery, not just antibiotic escalation.
Outpatient treatment is appropriate only after clinical stability and complication control have been established.
Treatment decisions should be made with a multidisciplinary endocarditis team whenever possible.
European Society of Cardiology — 2023 ESC Guidelines for the management of endocarditis.
American Heart Association — 2026 Scientific Statement: Infective Endocarditis—Diagnosis, Antibiotic Therapy, and Management.

blocks.text: Prescribing note: This is a clinical reference, not a substitute for patient-specific prescribing. IE regimens should be finalised with cardiology and microbiology/infectious diseases input, with local resistance data, product labelling and renal/hepatic function taken into account.
